source_title: National Park Service — Grand Canyon geology
facts: The Grand Canyon's exposed rocks record nearly two billion years of Earth's history.
The Grand Canyon is far younger than the rocks forming its walls.
Ancient seas left limestone layers high in today's Grand Canyon walls.
Lava has cascaded down the Grand Canyon's walls during volcanic eruptions.
The Grand Canyon's cliffs and slopes differ because some rock layers resist erosion better than others.
Much of the Grand Canyon's missing dinosaur-age rock was removed by erosion.
Nearly forty identified rock layers make up the Grand Canyon's walls.
The Colorado River cut downward faster than the dry landscape could widen into a broad valley.
The Grand Canyon's oldest exposed rocks were transformed by intense heat and pressure.
Some tilted rock layers in the Grand Canyon record ancient mountain building followed by erosion.

source_title: National Park Service — Yellowstone hydrothermal features
facts: Yellowstone contains more than 500 geysers, the greatest concentration on Earth.
Microbes create many of the vivid colours around Yellowstone's hot springs.
Different temperature-loving microbes form different coloured bands around a hot spring.
Geysers erupt because narrow underground passages trap heat and pressure.
Yellowstone's Steamboat Geyser can throw water more than 90 metres high.
Old Faithful does not erupt at exactly the same interval every time.
The rotten-egg smell around Yellowstone mudpots comes from hydrogen sulfide.
Microbes help turn rock into clay in Yellowstone's bubbling mudpots.
Yellowstone's travertine terraces grow as spring water deposits dissolved limestone.
Some Yellowstone steam vents hiss because their water boils away before reaching the surface.
The Great Barrier Reef is a network of thousands of reefs, not one continuous wall.
The Great Barrier Reef World Heritage area includes more than 900 islands.
Six of the world's seven sea-turtle species occur in the Great Barrier Reef region.
The Great Barrier Reef includes deep ocean water as well as shallow coral gardens.
Raine Island is a globally important nesting ground for green turtles.
Corals on the Great Barrier Reef release eggs and sperm in spectacular mass-spawning events.
The Great Barrier Reef's seagrass meadows feed dugongs.
During past ice ages, lower sea levels exposed parts of the Great Barrier Reef as limestone hills.
The Great Barrier Reef supports over 1,500 fish species.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have longstanding cultural connections with the Great Barrier Reef.
Victoria Falls spans the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe.
The Zambezi plunges across a curtain roughly 1.7 kilometres wide at Victoria Falls.
Spray from Victoria Falls can be visible from tens of kilometres away.
Victoria Falls sustains a small rainforest through its constant spray.
The gorges below Victoria Falls trace earlier positions of the waterfall.
Victoria Falls cuts into basalt, a rock formed from volcanic lava.
Victoria Falls' downstream gorges follow a striking zigzag course.
Islands along Victoria Falls divide its curtain into separate sections.
The rock gorges near Victoria Falls provide nesting sites for rare birds.
Victoria Falls keeps changing as erosion cuts back into the rock.
Fog supplies the main source of water in the Namib Sand Sea.
Namib dune sand travelled through rivers, ocean currents and wind before reaching the desert.
Young, moving dunes cover an older dune system in the Namib Sand Sea.
Some Namib animals escape surface heat by diving into loose sand.
The Namib Sand Sea lies beside the Atlantic Ocean.
Changing winds continually reshape the Namib's dunes.
The Namib Sand Sea includes a coastal lagoon as well as dunes.
Some Namib species live nowhere else, having evolved for its fog-fed desert.
Temporary rivers occur even in the extremely dry Namib Sand Sea.
Rocky hills stand like islands within the Namib's sea of sand.

source_title: UNESCO — Palace and Park of Versailles
facts: Versailles grew from a smaller château built by Louis XIII.
Louis XIV expanded Versailles into both a royal home and a centre of government.
Versailles' gardens were designed by André Le Nôtre.
The Hall of Mirrors sits between rooms devoted to War and Peace.
Versailles influenced the design of royal residences across Europe.
Marie-Antoinette had a picturesque hamlet built within the Versailles estate.
The Petit Trianon at Versailles was designed by Jacques-Ange Gabriel.
The Versailles estate took roughly a century and a half of royal building work to develop.
Versailles' gardens use long sightlines, water and geometry to extend the palace's architecture outdoors.
The Versailles World Heritage property includes the Trianon palaces, not just the main palace.
